# Do Springs Wear Out?

When you're swapping out struts and shocks on a vehicle, it's tempting to treat the springs as disposable components simply because they've seen high mileage. In your specific case, replacing suspension dampers at 80,000 km while leaving the original springs installed—now sitting at nearly 200,000 km—is a common scenario that invites technical scrutiny. The core question isn't whether springs "wear out" in the sense of friction or corrosion; it is whether they have lost their dynamic properties due to material fatigue or permanent deformation.

Springs operate under constant cyclic loading. Every time your wheel hits a bump, the spring compresses and rebounds. This repetitive stress causes metal fatigue over an extended period. Unlike shock absorbers, which contain hydraulic fluid that degrades, corrodes, or loses viscosity, coil springs are solid steel (or sometimes chrome-molybdenum alloy). They don't leak, and they don't break down chemically in the same way fluid-filled systems do. However, the microscopic crystal structure of the metal does change with every compression cycle.

The primary failure mode for a spring at 200,000 km is not usually a sudden snap, but rather a loss of stiffness or a reduction in ride height due to permanent set. If the spring has "bottomed out" repeatedly during its life—meaning it hit the limit of travel without sufficient damping from the shock—it may have undergone plastic deformation. In engineering terms, this means the material has moved past its elastic limit and will no longer return to its original length perfectly.

Visually inspecting a spring for cracks or rust is only part of the diagnostic process. Rust on the coils can be superficial, but severe corrosion reduces the cross-sectional area of the wire, effectively lowering the spring rate (stiffness). A stiffer spring alters the vehicle's handling balance and can lead to uneven tire wear. More critically, if the spring has lost its ability to return fully to its resting length, it changes the static ride height. This shifts the suspension geometry, affecting camber and toe settings even if you align the car after installation.

From a maintenance strategy perspective, mixing old springs with new dampers introduces variables that are hard to tune out. New shocks rely on specific damping characteristics tuned for a certain spring rate and mass. If your old springs have settled or stiffened slightly over 120,000 km of additional use, the new dampers might not perform as intended. You could end up with an overly harsh ride if the springs are too stiff, or poor body control if they have lost tension.

If you decide to keep the existing springs, you must verify that the static ride height matches the manufacturer's specification within a few millimeters. If there is significant sag, the suspension geometry is compromised regardless of alignment adjustments. In many professional shops, replacing both sets simultaneously is considered best practice because it restores the original design parameters and ensures predictable behavior under load.

There are exceptions where springs can be reused. If they show no signs of corrosion, have maintained their height, and the vehicle has been driven on smooth roads with consistent tire pressure, a spring at 200,000 km might still function acceptably. However, this is a gamble against material fatigue limits that aren't always visible to the naked eye.
